label: Variations of Energy
notes: This chapter, printed pages 191 through 209, recasts geodesics as critical points of an energy functional. We develop first and second variation formulas, the index form, conjugate points through Jacobi fields, and close with the Bonnet-Myers compactness theorem that positive curvature forces on a complete manifold.

label: The Energy Functional
notes: Energy weights speed quadratically, unlike arc length, which makes it differentiable and minimized exactly by constant-speed parametrizations. Cauchy-Schwarz gives length squared at most twice energy times interval length, with equality precisely for constant speed, so minimizing energy chooses both shortest path and uniform pacing.

label: Variations of a Curve
notes: A proper variation is a smooth family of curves sharing the same endpoints, indexed by a parameter that deforms the base curve. Its variational field measures the transverse velocity at parameter zero, and differentiating energy along the family converts geometry into a single ordinary derivative we can evaluate.

label: First Variation Formula
notes: Differentiating energy and integrating by parts splits the result into an interior integral against the acceleration field plus boundary terms. The interior term measures geodesic curvature, while the boundary term records endpoint motion, cleanly separating where a curve fails to be straight from how its ends move.

label: Geodesics Are Critical Points
notes: For proper variations the boundary term vanishes, so the first variation is zero for every admissible field exactly when the covariant acceleration vanishes identically. Thus geodesics are precisely the critical points of energy among curves with fixed endpoints, the variational characterization underpinning the entire chapter.

label: Energy Along a Variation
notes: Plotting energy against the variation parameter near a geodesic yields a curve whose slope vanishes at the origin, confirming criticality. Whether that critical point is a genuine minimum or merely a saddle is decided by the second derivative, which motivates computing the second variation formula next.

label: Second Variation Formula
notes: The second derivative of energy at a geodesic equals the index form evaluated on the variational field. It pairs the squared covariant derivative of the field against a curvature term, exposing exactly how sectional curvature governs whether nearby curves cost more or less energy than the geodesic.

label: The Index Form
notes: The index form is a symmetric bilinear form on fields vanishing at the endpoints, built from the covariant derivative and curvature. Its definiteness decides stability: positive definite means the geodesic locally minimizes energy, while any negative direction exhibits a shorter nearby competitor and certifies instability.

label: Jacobi Fields and Conjugate Points
notes: Nontrivial fields in the kernel of the index form solve the Jacobi equation, linking second variation to the geodesic deviation studied earlier. Endpoints joined by such a field vanishing at both ends are conjugate, marking where neighbouring geodesics refocus and where minimization can first break down.

label: Past a Conjugate Point
notes: Beyond the first conjugate point the index form acquires a negative direction, so the geodesic no longer minimizes energy. An explicit variation built from the Jacobi field, cut and rescaled, produces a strictly shorter neighbouring curve, visually a transverse push that lowers energy past the focal point.

label: Bonnet-Myers Theorem
notes: If Ricci curvature is bounded below by a positive constant, the second variation applied to long geodesics forces a negative index direction, contradicting minimality beyond a fixed length. Hence a complete manifold with such curvature has diameter at most pi over the square root of that bound, making it compact.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: Energy variation converts geodesics into critical points, second variation and the index form measure stability, and Jacobi fields locate conjugate points where minimization fails. Bonnet-Myers shows curvature controls global size, while Synge-Weinstein refines the topology, themes carried into the comparison theorems that follow.
